stops.name: Vienna, the Master; the task is set
stops.campa: Felix the emissary leads to another, whom Steiner will never name, calling him only the M., the Master. From this personality the student receives his life's commission: the stream of the spirit must be led into the age of natural science not against the current of materialism but through it; he must first master the thinking of the time in order to redeem it, must clothe the ancient knowledge in forms the modern mind can test. The meeting leaves no document and needs none. From this hour the biography moves like a man under orders.
stops.quote: I did not meet the M. at once, but first an emissary sent by him, who was completely initiated into the secrets of the plant world.
stops.quote_source: Autobiographical sketch for Édouard Schuré (the Barr Document), September 1907

stops.name: Vienna, Kürschner's call: the Goethe edition
stops.campa: On Schröer's recommendation, Joseph Kürschner of Stuttgart summons a twenty-one-year-old student, without doctorate or name, to edit Goethe's scientific writings for the Deutsche National-Litteratur: the poet's botany, his optics, his metamorphosis of plants, the part of Goethe the professors dismiss. The unknown youth is set to introduce Goethe the scientist to the German nation. He accepts as one who recognizes his orders arriving by post. In Goethe's way of seeing, the archetypal plant beheld within the plants, he finds the seed of the epistemology he must build: the training of exact clairvoyance.

stops.name: Vienna, the Specht household; the sleeping soul awakened
stops.campa: In July 1884 he enters the house of the cotton merchant Ladislaus Specht as tutor to four sons. The youngest, Otto, ten years old, is hydrocephalic, judged ineducable; the least effort of thought brings headache and pallor. The tutor takes the case as a sacred problem: he prepares each half-hour lesson for hours, shaping every step to the child's hidden soul, economizing the boy's forces like a physician of the spirit. Within two years the great head visibly diminishes; the boy enters the Gymnasium. Otto Specht will become a doctor of medicine. In this sickroom pedagogy the Waldorf school is conceived, thirty-five years before Stuttgart.
stops.quote: I had to find access to a soul which was, as it were, in a sleeping state.

stops.name: Vienna, the salon of Marie Eugenie delle Grazie
stops.campa: At the Saturday evenings of the poetess delle Grazie he sits among Catholic theologians of the university, Cistercians among them: Wilhelm Neumann, of whom he will say that one could speak with him of anything in heaven or earth and be met with learning and grace. The hostess reads her pessimist epics against the divine order; the priests defend it; the young Goethean, welcome to all parties and belonging to none, learns the countenance of Catholic scholarship at its noblest. Here he watches theology and modern despair contend, and measures the bridge that neither can build and he must.

stops.name: Vienna, the Goethe-Verein lecture: a new aesthetics
stops.campa: Before the Vienna Goethe Society the twenty-seven-year-old delivers his first great public utterance: Goethe as Father of a New Aesthetics. Beauty, he declares, is not the idea in sensible garment, as the professors teach, but the sensible raised into the garment of the spirit; art is not imitation of the divine but its continuation; the artist does not copy creation, he carries it further. In one evening the whole later Goetheanum stands in thought: a building will one day be raised on a hill in Switzerland to say in wood and glass what this lecture says in words.

stops.name: Weimar, the Goethe-Schiller Archive
stops.campa: In the autumn of 1890 he arrives in the city of Goethe to serve seven years in the Goethe-Schiller Archive, summoned to edit the natural-scientific manuscripts for the great Sophien edition. The archive stands above the Ilm like a temple of the German spirit; in its folders lie Goethe's own hand: the botany, the color studies, the bone of the skull traced in the Jewish cemetery of Venice. Daily he handles the pages as a priest handles relics, and daily disputes with the philologists who count commas where he reads a method of seeing. Weimar is his monastery; the manuscripts are his liturgy.

stops.name: Rostock, the doctorate
stops.campa: He travels north to the Baltic, to Rostock, where Heinrich von Stein, the old philosopher who wrote of the seven books of Platonism, examines him at six in the evening of 23 October in philosophy, mathematics and mechanics. The dissertation, on the fundamental question of epistemology with regard to Fichte's doctrine of the ego, becomes the book Truth and Knowledge, dedicated to Eduard von Hartmann: consciousness is not walled off from being; in thinking, the world itself comes to presence. Three days later the archive editor is Doctor of Philosophy. The credentials of the age are being gathered, one by one, by the emissary sent into the age.

stops.name: Weimar, the house of Anna Eunike
stops.campa: He takes rooms in the house of Anna Eunike, a widow with five children, and finds there the first hearth of his adult life. She keeps his impossible hours, guards his study, mothers the philosopher who forgets to eat. In her household the homeless thinker writes his masterwork. The friendship will follow him to Berlin and become marriage; the canon honors her quietly, the woman who kept the door of the room in which the Philosophy of Freedom was written.

stops.name: Weimar, Die Philosophie der Freiheit is published
stops.campa: In November 1893 the book of his life appears: The Philosophy of Freedom, results of soul-observation by the method of natural science. Against Kant's barrier he sets the deed of thinking, which no barrier can bind because it is itself the world's own activity awake in man; freedom is not given, but achieved whenever a man acts from intuitions he himself brings forth. The age ignores the book. Its author knows what he has written: the foundation on which everything to come, the occult science, the schools, the building, will stand. All anthroposophy, he will insist, is contained in it as the plant in the seed.
stops.quote: To live in love towards our actions, and to let live in the understanding of the other person's will, is the fundamental maxim of free human beings.
stops.quote_source: Die Philosophie der Freiheit (1894), ch. IX

stops.name: Jena, Haeckel's sixtieth birthday
stops.campa: He goes over the hills to Jena for the sixtieth birthday of Ernst Haeckel, the apostle of Darwin, the terror of the theologians. The two men take to each other: the monist who denies the spirit and the seer who affirms it find common cause in the honesty of evolution against the dishonesty of dogma. Steiner will defend Haeckel publicly for years, to the scandal of both camps, for he sees in the doctrine of evolution the torso of a true spiritual fact: what natural science traces in the flesh, spiritual science completes in the soul. One must go through Haeckel, he says, and beyond him.

stops.name: Naumburg, Nietzsche's sickroom
stops.campa: Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, who has engaged the young doctor to order her brother's library, leads him up to the sickroom at Naumburg. On a couch in the darkened chamber lies Friedrich Nietzsche, mad these seven years, gazing without seeing. Steiner stands before him and beholds, with the eyes the waiting room at Pottschach opened, Nietzsche's soul hovering above the head, radiant, already loosed from the body, held to earth by a thread, a soul that in the body could not find its world. He leaves the room bearing the image; from it comes his book on Nietzsche, the fighter for freedom against his time.
stops.quote: There lay Nietzsche upon a couch... with the beautiful forehead, the forehead of an artist and a thinker in one.

stops.name: Weimar, Goethes Weltanschauung; the farewell
stops.campa: He closes the seven Weimar years with the book Goethe's World-Conception, the harvest of the archive: Goethe stands revealed not as poet who dabbled in science but as the founder of a new way of knowing, the contemplation that sees the idea in the phenomenon as the eye sees color. The manuscripts are edited, the introductions written, the apprenticeship among the relics of the German spirit is complete. He is thirty-six, unknown, and finished with preparation. He packs for Berlin, out of the city of the dead Goethe into the roaring capital of the living age, where the spirit must now be spoken, not curated.
